decisionSource: The enrolled Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 as published by the Oregon Legislature, retrieved and hashed in this job; the complete version chain of House Bill 3825 as published on the Legislature's own OLIS measure-document channel, from Introduced through A-Engrossed and B-Engrossed to Enrolled; the current codified text of ORS 18.194, ORS 18.180, ORS 137.225 and ORS 475C.397 in the Legislature's 2025 Edition; the Legislature's 2025 and 2026 Oregon Laws amended-and-repealed tables; and the Legislature's own statement of what the 2025 Edition does and does not carry. Read against the integrated Oregon legal-design memo, the normalized track registry and the authoritative blocker ledger.
whatThisDocumentIs: The decision record that fixes the reach of Oregon's 2025 monetary-obligations relief. The integrated Oregon memo carries, on or_conviction_setaside, a release blocker recording that the controlling review describes Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1 as a general rule — that expired judgment remedies for monetary obligations in any judgment of conviction count as sentence completion — while the enrolled text read on 2026-08-06 appeared narrower, and that the difference between those readings is the difference between a broad unlock and a marijuana-specific one. This record settles it from the enacted text and from the act's own legislative history. It amends no memo, regenerates no registry, implements nothing, enables nothing and asserts no counsel approval.

scopeOfThisJob.siblingJobNotTouched: The Oregon same-episode question is a separate frozen job, rcap-or-same-episode-rule-source-reconciliation, with its own owned decision record. It shares two affected tracks with this one and is not resolved, narrowed or prejudged here.

questionPresented.theConflict: The controlling review describes Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1 as a general rule: that expired judgment remedies for monetary obligations in any judgment of conviction count as sentence completion for set-aside purposes. The enrolled text is narrower in its operative first subsection, which expires the judgment remedies only for a judgment entered in a municipal court or justice court for a pre-July 1, 2015 marijuana-possession offence under one ounce. Subsection (2) then applies the sentence-completion consequence to obligations that have expired 'under subsection (1) of this section'.
questionPresented.thePivot: Whether the consequence in subsection (2) reaches obligations that expire under ORS 18.194 generally, or only those expired by subsection (1).
questionPresented.whyItMattered: Sentence completion is the gate on the whole conviction set-aside route. ORS 137.225(1)(a) opens the remedy only to a person 'who has fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court'. On the broad reading, an unpaid balance on an old judgment stops being a bar for a large population; on the narrow reading it stops being a bar for a small and specific one. A screening question that promises the first and delivers the second tells people they are eligible when they are not.

methodNote: Three commitments. First, the enrolled act was retrieved and hashed in this job rather than relied on from a prior reading, and its complete text is reproduced below: it is one page and two sections, so completeness is verifiable rather than asserted. Second, where an attorney review and an enacted text diverge, the divergence is explained rather than merely scored — the act's own version chain was read from Introduced forward, because a review describing a rule the enacted text does not contain is usually describing an earlier draft, and here it demonstrably was. Third, the negative propositions — that no other section of the act broadens it, that nothing later amended it, and that ORS 137.225 carries no independent monetary rule — are each established affirmatively from the Legislature's own amended-and-repealed tables and from a full-text reading of the codified section, not from failure to find.

controllingSources.citation: Oregon Laws 2025, chapter 395 (House Bill 3825), Relating to monetary obligations in criminal cases
controllingSources.completeness: The act is one page and contains exactly two sections. The whole of it is reproduced here, so nothing is summarised and nothing is omitted.
controllingSources.verbatimText: CHAPTER 395 — AN ACT — HB 3825 — Relating to monetary obligations in criminal cases; and prescribing an effective date. Be It Enacted by the People of the State of Oregon: SECTION 1. (1) Notwithstanding ORS 18.194, judgment remedies for a judgment of conviction entered in a municipal court or justice court for violating, prior to July 1, 2015, a city or county ordinance or state statute prohibiting the possession of less than one ounce of marijuana, that have not yet expired under the provisions of ORS 18.194, expire on the effective date of this 2025 Act. (2) If the judgment remedies for monetary obligations in a judgment of conviction have expired under subsection (1) of this section, a person shall be considered to have completed, fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court with respect to those monetary obligations for purposes of ORS 137.225 or 475C.397 or any other statute authorizing the court to set aside the judgment of conviction. SECTION 2. This 2025 Act takes effect on the 91st day after the date on which the 2025 regular session of the Eighty-third Legislative Assembly adjourns sine die. Approved by the Governor June 24, 2025. Filed in the office of Secretary of State June 24, 2025. Effective date September 26, 2025.
controllingSources.relatingClauseFinding: The relating clause is 'Relating to monetary obligations in criminal cases; and prescribing an effective date.' It contains no 'amending ORS' phrase and no 'creating new provisions' phrase. The act amends nothing and creates no codified section.

controllingSources.citation: House Bill 3825, 83rd Oregon Legislative Assembly, 2025 Regular Session — Introduced, A-Engrossed, B-Engrossed and Enrolled
controllingSources.issuer: Oregon Legislative Assembly, OLIS measure-document channel
controllingSources.operativeFinding: The general rule the review describes existed, and it was removed. The Introduced bill's relating clause was 'Relating to monetary obligations in criminal cases; creating new provisions; amending ORS 18.180 and 137.225'. Its section 1 amended ORS 18.180, the circuit-court expiration section, to cut criminal-judgment remedies from twenty years to ten for a felony and five for a misdemeanour, and its digest read: 'Shortens the time period after which judgment remedies for monetary obligations in criminal judgments without restitution expire. Provides that the expiration of judgment remedies means that a person has complied with that portion of a sentence for purposes of expungement.' That is the review's description almost word for word. The A-Engrossed, ordered by the House April 10, brackets every one of those digest lines as deleted, drops ORS 18.180 from the relating clause, and replaces section 1 with the marijuana-only expiration; its new digest reads 'The Act makes judgment remedies for some marijuana convictions in local courts expire.' The B-Engrossed, including Senate amendments dated May 27, deleted the surviving ORS 137.225 amendment, dropped 'creating new provisions; amending ORS 137.225' from the relating clause, folded the deeming rule into section 1(2) as freestanding uncodified law, and added 'prior to July 1, 2015' to section 1(1). The B-Engrossed section 1 is character-identical to the Enrolled section 1, which was verified by direct comparison of the extracted operative text.
controllingSources.whyThisMatters: It explains the conflict rather than merely resolving it. The review is not wrong about a law; it is describing the introduced draft's digest, which was superseded in the first round of House amendments. That is a materially different kind of error from a misreading, and it means the review's other statements sourced to the same draft should be treated with the same caution.

controllingSources.citation: ORS 18.194, Expiration and extension of judgment remedies for justice and municipal court judgments
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Subsection (3): judgment remedies for a judgment in a criminal action in a justice or municipal court expire twenty years after entry of the judgment, and fifty years where the judgment includes a money award for restitution. Subsection (9): the judgment remedies for a judgment in a criminal action may not be extended under the section. The section governs justice and municipal courts only.

controllingSources.citation: ORS 18.180, Expiration of judgment remedies (circuit court)
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Subsection (4): judgment remedies for a judgment in a criminal action expire twenty years after entry, and fifty years where the judgment includes a money award for restitution. This is the circuit-court section. Chapter 395 does not mention it and did not amend it; the Introduced bill's amendment to it was the first thing the House removed.

controllingSources.citation: ORS 137.225, Order setting aside conviction or record of arrest, citation or charge
controllingSources.issuer: Oregon Legislative Assembly, 2025 Edition; source credit ends '2024 c.70 §55; 2025 c.349 §1'
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Subsection (1)(a) is the eligibility hook and it is the only place monetary obligations bite: relief is open to a person 'who has fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court', and 'A person who is still under supervision as part of the sentence for the offense that is the subject of the motion has not fully complied with or performed the sentence of the court.' The section's only other monetary reference is in subsection (3)(a), and it runs the other way and concerns the court's public-safety weighing rather than eligibility: 'The court may not consider nonpunitive civil liability, monetary obligations and motor vehicle violations.' A full-text reading of all thirteen subsections returns no occurrence of 'judgment remedies', '18.194', 'expire', 'money award', 'restitution', 'unpaid', 'balance' or 'outstanding'.
controllingSources.consequence: ORS 137.225 contains no independent rule about monetary obligations, their payment or their expiration. The whole of the monetary-obligation bridge into sentence completion is supplied by the uncodified chapter 395 note, which is why the scope of that note decides the question.

controllingSources.citation: ORS 475C.397, Order setting aside qualifying marijuana conviction
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Subsection (7)(b) defines a 'qualifying marijuana conviction' as a conviction for a marijuana offence based on conduct described in ORS 475C.305 or possession of less than one ounce, committed prior to July 1, 2015, and 'For which the person has completed and fully complied with or performed the sentence of the court'. That third element is precisely what chapter 395 section 1(2) supplies for the monetary component.
controllingSources.retrievalNote: This section had defeated earlier retrieval attempts from the Legislature's own channel. It is served at ors475C.html with a capital C in the filename; a lower-case ors475c.html does not resolve. Recorded so the next worker does not repeat the failure.

controllingSources.citation: Oregon Laws 2025 and Oregon Laws 2026 tables of sections amended, repealed or added to, and the 2025 special session table
controllingSources.operativeFinding: The 2025 table carries no entry for chapter 395 at all, which is how an act that amends nothing appears; it also shows ORS 18.194 and ORS 475C.397 unamended in the 2025 regular session and ORS 137.225 amended only by chapter 349. The 2026 table carries no entry for ORS 18.194, ORS 137.225 or ORS 475C.397, and its separate table of sections in uncodified law amended, repealed or added to — which is where an amendment to 2025 chapter 395 section 1 would have to appear, and which does list many other 2025 chapters — carries no entry for chapter 395. The 2025 special session table carries no relevant entry.
controllingSources.whyItMatters: This is what makes 'nothing later broadened it' an affirmative finding. An uncodified session-law section cannot be tracked through the ORS, so the uncodified-law table is the only instrument that would show an amendment, and it shows none.

controllingSources.citation: Oregon Revised Statutes publication page, Oregon Legislative Assembly
controllingSources.operativeFinding: The Legislature states: 'The 2025 Edition does not include changes to the law enacted during the 2025 special session or the 2026 regular session'; that those changes will appear in the 2027 Edition; that a reader must examine the 2025 Edition together with the 2025 special session Oregon Laws and 2026 Oregon Laws for the most up-to-date law; and that 'The official text is the printed published copy of the Oregon Revised Statutes. The database-is-not-official caveat is recorded rather than suppressed; the enrolled session law, which carries no such caveat, is the primary authority for the operative holding.

determination.1_isSubsection2GeneralOrMarijuanaLimited: Marijuana-limited. The sentence-completion consequence in Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1(2) reaches only those monetary obligations whose judgment remedies expired by operation of section 1(1). It does not reach obligations that expire under ORS 18.194 generally, and it reaches nothing under ORS 18.180 at all.
2_whyTheTextCompelsThat: The trigger is a closed internal cross-reference. Subsection (2) operates where remedies 'have expired under subsection (1) of this section'. The only remedies that ever expire under subsection (1) are the ones subsection (1) itself extinguishes, and subsection (1) is exhaustively specific. The class reached by (2) cannot be larger than the class extinguished by (1).

The drafter demonstrably knew how to write the general reference and chose not to. Subsection (1) opens 'Notwithstanding ORS 18.194'. The same drafter, in the adjacent subsection, wrote 'under subsection (1) of this section' rather than 'under ORS 18.194'. The contrast is deliberate and is the clearest internal evidence in the act.

The phrase that reads broadly governs a different variable. 'for purposes of ORS 137.225 or 475C.397 or any other statute authorizing the court to set aside the judgment of conviction' sits in the consequence clause. It broadens which set-aside statutes may receive the deemed compliance; it does not broaden which obligations qualify. The indefinite article in 'monetary obligations in a judgment of conviction' is likewise qualified by the trigger that follows it.

The legislative history removes any residual doubt. The general rule was in the Introduced bill, keyed to ORS 18.180, and the House deleted it on April 10. Reading subsection (2) broadly would restore by construction the very provision the Legislature struck.
determination.3_whatTheReliefReaches: Monetary obligations in a judgment of conviction where all four of these hold: the judgment was entered in an Oregon municipal court or justice court, not a circuit court; it was for violating a city or county ordinance or state statute prohibiting possession of less than one ounce of marijuana; the violation occurred before July 1, 2015, the date modifying 'violating' rather than the entry of judgment, which matches the parallel wording of ORS 475C.397(7)(b)(B); and the judgment remedies had not already expired under ORS 18.194 as at September 26, 2025. Where all four hold, the remedies expired on September 26, 2025 and the person is deemed to have completed, fully complied with and performed the sentence with respect to those monetary obligations for the purposes of ORS 137.225, ORS 475C.397 and any other set-aside statute.
4_whatItDoesNotReach: Circuit court convictions of any kind, including marijuana convictions. ORS 18.180 governs the circuit courts and was left untouched. This is the largest limitation by population, because most Oregon criminal convictions are circuit court.
Any non-marijuana municipal or justice court conviction — traffic, other ordinance violations, other misdemeanours.
Marijuana convictions for one ounce or more, and marijuana delivery or manufacture convictions.

The debt itself. The act expires judgment remedies, which are the enforcement mechanisms; it does not vacate, forgive or discharge the underlying obligation and it orders no refund. The Introduced bill's vacatur provision was deleted. Subsection (2) creates a deemed sentence completion for set-aside purposes only, and says so twice — 'with respect to those monetary obligations' and 'for purposes of'.
Any other component of the sentence. Outstanding supervision still defeats eligibility under the second sentence of ORS 137.225(1)(a), and the deeming clause does not touch it.
determination.5_effectiveDateAndApplicability: Approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on June 24, 2025; effective September 26, 2025, being the 91st day after sine die, as computed and printed by Legislative Counsel on the face of the session law. The act contains no applicability clause, no savings clause and no emergency clause. The only temporal limits are internal to section 1(1).
determination.6_codificationStatus: Uncodified. Section 1 was never added to the ORS. Legislative Counsel prints it as an editorial note in three places — following ORS 18.194, following ORS 137.225 and following ORS 475C.397 — each carrying the bracketed effective date '[September 26, 2025]' and the citation '[2025 c.395 §1]'. The 2025 amended-and-repealed table carries no entry for chapter 395, which is the expected appearance for an act that amends nothing.
determination.7_hasAnythingLaterChangedIt: No. Oregon held a 2026 regular session and it did not touch these provisions: the 2026 amended-and-repealed table shows no entry for ORS 18.194, ORS 137.225 or ORS 475C.397, and its table of uncodified sections amended, repealed or added to carries no entry for 2025 chapter 395. The 2026 acts that do touch the neighbouring chapters are chapter 14, a driving-while-suspended omnibus, and chapter 118, a medical-marijuana measure, neither of which reaches this relief. Chapter 395 stands exactly as enacted.
determination.8_isTheReviewWrong: Yes, and identifiably so. The review is describing the digest of the Introduced bill, which did contain a general rule keyed to ORS 18.180. That rule was deleted by House amendment on April 10, 2025 and never became law. The review is not misreading the enacted text; it is reading a superseded draft.

9_affectedOregonTracks.or_conviction_setaside: Directly affected. It carries the release blocker in terms and it carries the participant input cvsMonetaryObligations, whose condition description currently says chapter 395 'treats monetary obligations whose judgment remedies have expired as satisfied for sentence-completion purposes, on the narrow terms recorded in the unresolved questions'. That framing is right to be cautious and is now capable of being made precise.
9_affectedOregonTracks.or_contempt_setaside: Affected through its own cntMonetaryObligations input, which carries the same condition description. This track is a contempt-finding route under ORS 137.225(1)(b)(B) and (1)(b)(D); a contempt finding is not a marijuana possession conviction entered in a municipal or justice court, so chapter 395 will essentially never operate on it. The input is not wrong to exist, because a participant may have such a judgment on another case, but the relief is not a contempt-route mechanism.
9_affectedOregonTracks.or_marijuana_setaside: Affected, and it is the one track where the relief actually does work. It is deferred under legal_research_required and stays deferred: this record does not resolve its build blockers. It does close, on the merits, the part of its release question that asked what the municipal and justice court expiration relief is and whether it is automatic — it is automatic, by operation of law, and it happened on September 26, 2025.
9_affectedOregonTracks.notAffected: or_arrest_no_charges, or_dismissed_charge, or_acquittal and or_137_225_1d are unaffected. None turns on sentence completion, because none involves a conviction; ORS 137.225(1)(c) and (1)(d) are the arrest, citation, dismissal and acquittal provisions and are available at any time. The six or-ls slots are unaffected.

determination.10_eligibilityAndScreeningImpact: The screening question survives but its consequence narrows sharply. cvsMonetaryObligations and cntMonetaryObligations may continue to be asked, and the answer may continue to route, but an unpaid balance may be treated as satisfied only where the four conditions in determination 3 are all met. The screen therefore needs two facts it does not currently collect: which court entered the judgment, municipal or justice as against circuit, and whether the offence was marijuana possession under one ounce committed before July 1, 2015. Without those two the relief cannot be applied without guessing, and guessing in the participant's favour would tell a circuit-court applicant that an unpaid fine is not a bar when it is.
determination.11_packetImpact: None to the generated documents. The relief operates by operation of law rather than by anything filed: nothing is submitted to trigger it, no form implements it and no additional component is required. Both affected implementable tracks are official_pdf_fill on the Oregon Judicial Department Criminal Set-Aside (Adult Cases) packet and their component sets are unchanged. The impact is confined to eligibility screening and to participant-facing copy, and there is one copy consequence worth stating: a packet must not tell a participant that expired judgment remedies mean their fines no longer count, without the municipal-or-justice-court and marijuana qualifications, because for most Oregon applicants that statement is false.
determination.12_buildLevelOrReleaseLevel: Release-level, and it was correctly classified as such in the memo. It does not change which document is generated, what goes on it, where it is filed or by whom; it changes what the product may tell a participant about their eligibility. Both affected implementable tracks remain implementable and neither becomes buildable-only-after-this. The correct disposition is that the release blocker can now be closed on the narrow reading rather than left open.
determination.13_doesThisCreateAnyRelief: No. This record creates nothing, and expressly does not read subsection (2) broadly in the participant's favour. The narrow reading is less favourable to more participants than the review's reading, and it is adopted because the text and the history compel it.

residualQuestions.question: Whether a marijuana municipal or justice court judgment whose remedies had already expired under ORS 18.194 before September 26, 2025 receives the deeming clause at all.
residualQuestions.analysis: On the text, apparently not. Subsection (1) reaches only remedies 'that have not yet expired', so remedies that had already lapsed did not expire 'under subsection (1)', and subsection (2)'s trigger is literally unmet. That would produce the anomaly that the staler record is the harder one to clear. This is a reading of the text arrived at in this job and is not stated by any official source; no Oregon court, Legislative Counsel note or agency guidance addressing it was located.
residualQuestions.whyNotABuildBlocker: It affects a sub-population of an already narrow class and changes only what the participant is told, not what is generated.
residualQuestions.owner: legal design, before release copy is written for or_marijuana_setaside

residualQuestions.question: Whether any Oregon appellate decision, Oregon Judicial Department form, Uniform Trial Court Rule change or published OJD guidance construes chapter 395 section 1(2), and in particular whether any of them has adopted the broad reading in practice.
residualQuestions.analysis: Not searched in this job. The textual and historical answer is not in doubt, but practice could diverge from it, and a court or the Judicial Department adopting the broad reading would matter operationally even though it would not change the text. This is the most significant gap in this record.

residualQuestions.question: The codified sections were read in the Legislature's online 2025 Edition, which the Legislature itself states is not the official text; the official text is the printed edition.
residualQuestions.analysis: Inherent and low-consequence here. The operative holding rests on the enrolled session law, which is the Legislature's own publication of enacted law and carries no such caveat, and which was retrieved and hashed in this job. The codified sections are used for context and boundary rather than for the holding.

residualQuestions.question: The chapter 395 note was located following ORS 18.194, ORS 137.225 and ORS 475C.397, one occurrence each. The remaining ORS chapters were not swept for a fourth placement.
residualQuestions.analysis: Three placements correspond exactly to the three ORS sections the act cites, so a fourth is unlikely. Recorded so the coverage claim is bounded rather than absolute.

terminalDispositionDetail.why: The narrowest accurate result. It is not unresolved: the enacted text, the act's structure and its version chain all point the same way and the act is short enough to be read in full. It is not a broad unlock: the general rule was deleted before enactment. It is not build-level: nothing about what is generated changes.
terminalDispositionDetail.conflictResolution: The enacted text governs and the review's statement is superseded, with the reason identified — the review describes the Introduced bill's digest, not the law. Neither source was preferred for convenience: the review's account was traced to its origin before it was set aside.
